newsitem.title: USA: High court hears cable-TV law case.
newsitem.headline: High court hears cable-TV law case.

text.p: The cable-television industry and the Justice Department put forward their conflicting views to the Supreme Court over a law requiring cable operators to carry the broadcasts of local TV stations.
The industry, charging that the so-called must-carry law amounts to illegal censorship, urged the high court to throw it out.

The Justice Department urged the court to uphold the law, arguing that many cable operators would dump a local TV station in favour of their own programming that could bring in more advertising revenues.

The 1992 law requires cable operators to devote up to a third of their channels to local public and private broadcast stations which offer such fare as home shopping, religious and "infomercial" broadcasts beamed from low-power TV stations.
Arguing on behalf of the government, Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger said it was important "to preserve a healthy multiplicity of broadcast sources."
He said if local stations were excluded from cable, broadcasters would suffer financially and be unable to offer a diversity of over-their-air programmes to local audiences.
But the justices peppered Dellinger with questions and doubts, noting that from 1985-92 -- before the must-carry law took effect -- only 31 local stations went off the air.
"What is your response to that?" Chief Justice William Rehnquist demanded of Dellinger, noting the low number.
Justice Stephen Breyer, seen as a key swing vote in the case, complained that there was a lack of "empirical evidence" to back up some of the arguments in favour of the law.
The cable industry said that even though cable operators could offer more and more channels to subscribers, the increased number has failed to make more room for local broadcasters.

"Unfortunately, it has not become less and less of a problem," said attorney H. Bartow Farr, arguing on behalf of the industry. He said the growth in the number of cable programmers has outstripped the growth in new channels.
The high court agreed earlier this year to review a ruling by three federal judges last December. It was the second time the justices have addressed the must-carry issue.
In 1994, the high court sent the case back to the three-judge panel for a decision under a different standard on whether the law passes constitutional muster.
In a victory for broadcasters and the Justice Department, the judges still upheld the law. The high court is expected to rule in early 1997.
